Tasks Correctly Using Critical Context
For example, our improved models in Muse show a 2.4x reduction in forgetting critical information necessary for helping you achieve your goals.
Active Memory enables Muse and Meta AI to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant, making it easier to build off your past conversations.
November 6, 2026 · 2 minute read
Today, we’re introducing specialized versions of our existing models, trained using Muse Wonder, and rolling them out to people who use Muse and Meta AI.
Current and previous Muse models on the Personal Superintelligence Index: 47% and 38%.
In Muse, our models show a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks where unexpected issues arise.
With Muse Wonder, we introduced Active Memory and Active Focus.
We’ve trained our models to recognize what type of information is temporary versus permanent, to reason across time, and to distinguish between what is still relevant and what has become stale.

One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this Active Memory: carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.

Introducing Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full: Frontier Models for Agents

Real work also unfolds over time. That’s why we’ve built our new models to have Active Memory, the ability to carry what matters to you across conversations and bring back the details that are relevant to the task at hand.

MemoryBench is an internal benchmark that tests how accurately a model can recall critical information across long, complex multi-turn conversations of 64K to 100K tokens that span several individual facts, with distractor conversations and injected turns that conflict with or later update the target details.
An LLM judge scores each answer against weighted, question-specific rubric criteria.
PSI is an internal composite of seven personal and knowledge-work evaluations: Agents’ Last Exam, AutomationBench-AA, FocusBench, JobBench, GDP.pdf, VBT, and DRACO.

The model was trained on multilingual training data, with substantial representation across worldwide languages.
Internally generated competitor runs use common settings where practical but remain best-effort: prompts, tools, and runtime may not be optimally tuned for proprietary models.

The post contains no methodology for the Personal Superintelligence Index or the Active Memory Eval, no task counts, and no description of how the baseline for the 67% Active Focus figure was measured.
Both benchmarks are Meta’s own, and no third-party evaluation of the specialized models has been published.
On the Active Memory Eval, the share of tasks where the model failed to use critical context fell from 24% to 10%, and 24 divided by 10 gives exactly 2.4.
That matches the 2.4x reduction in forgetting that Meta reports for Muse, although the post presents the two figures separately and does not say whether they come from the same measurement.
Meta has not named the specialized models, described their size, published the methodology or task sets behind its two internal benchmarks, or released figures for Meta AI specifically.
The figures describe Muse; Meta gives no separate scores for Meta AI, even though the same models are rolling out there.
On an internal Active Memory evaluation, the model uses critical context correctly in 90% of tasks, up from 76%.
In its Active Memory evaluation, the current model correctly used critical context in 90% of tasks, compared with 76% for the previous model.
Read the 90% and 76% figures as results for the critical-context evaluation; the Personal Superintelligence Index is a separate measure.
